name: ARMoR (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the deaths new antibiotics reach, 55% in high-income countries (the model's access_hic_share) spread over the largest by their resistance deaths, the rest over the countries with most resistance deaths (GRAM 2021), each weighted by access: a judgment, as no source splits the deaths reached by country.
summary: ARMoR (the Alliance for Reducing Microbial Resistance) argues in Europe for paying drug makers for new antibiotics through subscriptions, so that new drugs get developed although they are kept in reserve. We count its spending from its launch in September 2023 to December 2025 against what it won: a voluntary framework for member states' joint subscriptions in the EU pharmaceutical package agreed in December 2025, which it had made its key ask, at a {{row:attribution_share_shared}} share of the campaigners' credit. If member states fund it, the extra antibiotics avert deaths from drug-resistant infections, mostly of older people, less what the payments cost those who pay. At the defaults it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000; the result is mostly uncertainty: whether member states ever fund the framework, how many drugs a reward brings and ARMoR's share of the credit are all judgments. Every branch is discounted for missing data, and its national advocacy and paid research won no change in the period, so they count as cost only.

Yearly payments under an EU joint subscription, if member states set one up (EUR)

source.title: ARMoR, Why the EU's antibiotic revenue guarantee scheme stalled and how to fix it (March 2025)
source.quote: The initiative was funded through EU4Health with a total budget of €40M split over a timeframe of 49 months.

rows.explainer: Our judgment. The framework is voluntary and unfunded: member states that join decide how much to pay. Anchors: the EU's earlier joint revenue guarantee for existing antibiotics, EUR 40 million over 49 months with 23 countries signed up, stalled; Italy's national fund holds EUR 100 million (Global AMR R&D Hub, Pull incentives by country); ARMoR's own fair-share figure for the EU is EUR 1–1.2 billion per new antibiotic (its response to the Council's position on the vouchers, August 2025), paid over about ten years. EUR 75 million a year, from EUR 10 million (a pilot's scale) to EUR 400 million (several drugs at the EU's fair share).

Deaths averted worldwide by 18 new antibiotics over 30 years (Silverman Bonnifield and Towse, 2022)

source.title: Silverman Bonnifield and Towse (Center for Global Development, December 2022), Estimating the EU's return on investment from an ambitious program to incentivize new antibiotics
source.quote: Over its full 30-year time horizon, the program averts 9.9 million deaths and 374.5 million DALYs, generating an ROI of 125 to 1.

rows.explainer: Silverman Bonnifield and Towse's estimate (Center for Global Development, 2022) for a G7 and EU pull incentive that brings 18 new antibiotics against six priority pathogens over 30 years: each drug, after four years in reserve, cuts deaths from those pathogens by 5% a year, its effect falling 2% a year as resistance builds, against deaths growing 2% a year. Read with the access share below, as the model counts every patient worldwide.

rows.label: New antibiotics behind those deaths

source.title: Silverman Bonnifield and Towse (Center for Global Development, December 2022), Estimating the EU's return on investment from an ambitious program to incentivize new antibiotics
source.quote: which would seek to generate a total of 18 new antibiotics over three decades to treat six priority pathogens

rows.explainer: The programme's 18 drugs over three decades.

rows.label: A new drug's lifetime deaths averted over its average in the study's 30 years
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The study's drugs arrive over the 30 years, so the average drug counts only part of its life inside the window; a drug's whole life adds the years after it (its effect fades 2% a year against deaths growing 2% a year, so a year of its life late on is worth about as much as one early). Against that, one more drug beyond a pipeline is worth less than the average one. The study's deaths are not discounted (37.7 DALYs a death, as GRAM's undiscounted burden). 1.5, from 1 to 2.5.

rows.label: Share of the deaths a new antibiotic could avert that happen where patients get it
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The study's figure counts patients everywhere. New antibiotics reach few countries: only the US, the UK, Sweden and France have more than seven of the last 18 (Outterson's count, cited by ARMoR), and high-income countries have about a ninth of the deaths resistance causes (GRAM 2021). ARMoR's own model takes 6.9% access in low- and middle-income countries today. 20%, from 10% to 40%.

rows.label: Share of the deaths new drugs reach that are in high-income countries
rows.explainer: Our judgment, from the access share's own figures: high-income countries have about a ninth of the deaths and get new drugs almost fully, the rest of the world about 7% of its deaths, so of the deaths reached about 0.11 ÷ (0.11 + 0.89 × 0.069), 64%, are in high-income countries, less where their access is incomplete. 55%, from 40% to 75%.

rows.label: Deaths averted per new antibiotic, over its life, where patients get it
rows.explainer: The study's deaths per drug × its lifetime × the share of patients reached.

rows.label: Value of a death at the world's ages of resistance deaths (units of value)
rows.explainer: The ages of the deaths antimicrobial resistance causes worldwide (facts: death_ages, GRAM 2021 and our split above five), each valued at GiveWell's weight for that age; the 50-and-over band split at 70 (@death_ages.amr_share_70plus_of_50plus), each part at the mean of its five-year weights (50–69 and 70–84). Stands for the deaths reached outside high-income countries.

rows.label: Value of a death at high-income countries' ages of resistance deaths (units of value)
rows.explainer: The ages of resistance deaths in high-income countries (facts: death_ages, our judgment from GRAM 2021: almost all at 50 and over, most at 70 and over), valued the same way.

rows.label: Value of a death from drug-resistant infection averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The deaths reached, by where they are: high-income countries' ages for their share, the world's for the rest, × the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: The shared share of resistance's burden that is illness rather than death (@death_ages.amr_yld_share), as a ratio to the deaths' share.

rows.label: Years from the first payments to a new drug's approval
rows.explainer: Our judgment. A larger reward moves drugs already in development, and late-stage antibacterial candidates take some 3 to 10 years to approval. 5 years, from 3 to 10.

rows.explainer: Our judgment. Good: joint procurement can also secure supply of existing antibiotics, which run short in Europe. Harm: a voluntary, unfunded scheme could stand in for a stronger, funded EU-wide reward and delay it. A little more good than harm: ×1.05, from ×0.85 to ×1.3.

rows.label: Hospital costs saved by the new drugs, per euro of reward that brings them

source.title: ARMoR, Updating our pull incentives cost-benefit analysis (February 2025)
source.quote: The healthcare savings over 10 years are €3.4 billion using CGD’s cost estimates versus only €596 million using the previous estimates at a cost of €2.7 billion.

rows.explainer: Treating fewer resistant infections saves health systems money, which nets against the payments. ARMoR's update of its EU analysis with the study's cost data: €3.4 billion saved over ten years against €2.7 billion paid, 1.26. The EU pays only its 34% share of the rewards, so the EU's own savings per euro of the whole reward are about 0.43; 1.26 stands for the savings of every health system the drugs reach, which are public money too, per euro of reward. The range (0.43, the EU alone, to 2) is ours: ten years of a programme of 18 drugs, ARMoR's own analysis.

Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Our judgment: how far the study's effect per drug holds. Its 5% cut a year in six pathogens' deaths per drug is a modelling assumption, not a measured effect. Its own sensitivity runs anchor the range: a 2% cut per drug takes the global return from 125:1 to 50:1 (0.4), faster resistance to the new drugs to 100:1 (0.8). Many infections are treated before the pathogen is known, so a reserve drug reaches fewer of them than its target pathogens' deaths. 0.6, from 0.3 to 1.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the share of what a joint subscription would do that needs this clause. Member states could pay for new antibiotics without it, nationally (as the UK, Sweden and Italy do) or under the EU's existing joint procurement agreement, and a joint scheme may draw money away from national ones. The years a won reform counts already take in that a scheme would come some day anyway (templates.md Convention 5). Half, from 20% to 80%.

rows.label: This charity's share among those who worked for the result
rows.explainer: Our judgment: ARMoR's share among those who campaigned for the clause, by their spending and staff time. The Parliament proposed it; the BEAM Alliance of antibiotic developers had asked for a voucher plus a subscription since 2022, and drug makers' associations, research funders and other NGOs pressed for pull incentives too, with far larger budgets. ARMoR made the subscription model its key ask, wrote analyses used in talks with ten governments and the G7, spoke at a Commission training for member states and coordinated a joint position of non-profits; no third party credits it with the clause. 5%, from 1% to 15%.
